title: MoQ for the Curious
text:
About this book
MoQ for the Curious explains how Media over QUIC delivers live content: how publishers name it, relays distribute it, and players keep it useful when the network slows.
The book introduces networking and media concepts as they are needed. A live lecture provides a running example, from the first subscription to playback and debugging.
Start reading: What, Why and How →

title: MoQ for the Curious
text:
Where to begin
The first chapter explains what MoQ is, why it is useful, and how five activities fit together: connect, discover, request, deliver, and present. It then shows how MoQ compares with WebRTC and maps those activities to the chapters ahead. Tracks, groups, and objects give those steps a shared vocabulary. The later chapters cover security, a first experiment, and debugging.
A fictional lecture runs through the examples. When a new term appears, we explain what it means and why it matters. The glossary is here whenever a word gets in the way.

title: 1  What, Why and How
text:
What is MoQ?
This chapter explains what MoQ does, why it is useful, and how its parts fit together. We will follow a publication from its publisher to a player, then compare that model with WebRTC and map it to the rest of the book.
Media over QUIC (MoQ) lets applications publish live content that other applications can subscribe to. A publisher can send content directly to subscribers or distribute it through relays. MoQ Transport (MOQT) is the protocol that defines how content is named, requested, and delivered. It runs over QUIC, a secure transport with multiple independent byte streams, either directly or through WebTransport.
This is a publish/subscribe model: one endpoint makes content available, and another asks to receive it. We will use a live lecture to follow that exchange throughout the book.
In our lecture, the lecturer is a publisher. Each viewer is a subscriber. The lecturer could send directly to every viewer, but that would make the lecturer’s upload connection carry another copy for each person who joins. Instead, the publisher can send to a relay, a server that forwards the content to interested viewers.
An endpoint can be both a publisher and a subscriber: a student can receive the lecture and publish microphone audio over the same session. A relay receives content upstream and publishes it downstream. See the draft’s role definitions.
To let the viewers make different choices, the publisher gives the pieces separate names. The lecturer’s audio can be one track, camera video another, and slides a third. A track contains individually identifiable pieces of data called objects. For example, a media format might place one compressed video frame in each object. The phone viewer requests the audio track; the laptop viewer requests audio and video.
A relay can also cache objects: keep copies so it can answer later requests. Someone joining the lecture may need content published a moment earlier to begin playback. If the relay has kept that content, it can supply it without asking the lecturer to send another copy.
Although media motivates this design, an object’s payload can also be application data. The transport handles names and delivery. The application and its media format agree on what the delivered bytes mean.

title: 1  What, Why and How
text:
Why use MoQ?
Live delivery has to balance three needs: reaching many viewers, starting playback for people who join late, and keeping slow connections from falling further behind. MoQ brings named content, relays, and delivery choices into one protocol.
Suppose the lecturer produces four megabits of media each second, but one viewer’s connection can carry only two. Each second adds more work to the queue. Waiting for every byte makes that viewer fall further behind the lecture.
Discarding arbitrary bytes is not a good solution either. Compressed video often describes how a picture differs from earlier pictures. If the decoder, the component reconstructing pictures, never receives one of those earlier pictures, later data may be unusable. To catch up, the receiver needs a place from which it can resume decoding.
MoQ gives content a structure that the distribution network can use. Objects belong to groups, and a media format can arrange those groups around useful starting points. A relay can recognize the boundaries, reuse objects requested by several viewers, and choose which work to send on each viewer’s connection. It can do this without decoding the pictures. QUIC supplies separate byte streams so that unrelated content need not all wait behind the same missing bytes. These are central ideas in the draft’s motivation and relay model.
These delivery decisions can serve different audiences through the same distribution system. Our lecture might have a few people speaking and thousands listening. Speakers may need very little delay to take turns, while listeners may accept a little more buffering to avoid interruptions. The same publication can serve both, with delivery decisions made along their different paths.

title: 1  What, Why and How
text:
How does MoQ work?
We can follow a publication through five activities:

Connect: establish a compatible session.
Discover: find the publication and its tracks.
Request: choose the content to receive.
Deliver: move objects to the subscriber.
Present: decode and play the media.

These activities give us a way to study the system. Some can overlap, and discovery may be unnecessary when names are already known. Each has a different job.

Connect: establish a session
The viewer connects to a server using QUIC or, in the browser path covered here, WebTransport. The endpoints agree on a MOQT version and exchange session settings. They now have a conversation in which they can make requests. QUIC and WebTransport explains the transport; Publishing and Subscribing explains the session.


Discover: find the content
The application turns the viewer’s choice of lecture into names. It may already know the publication or use discovery to find it. A media description then tells the player which tracks contain audio and video and how to interpret them. Tracks, Groups and Objects introduces names, and Media and the Browser explains the media description.


Request: choose what to receive
The viewer subscribes to the tracks it wants, such as audio and low-resolution video. A late arrival may also need earlier objects before playback can begin. The receiver can request retained content while following new objects. Publishing and Subscribing follows acceptance, late joining, and cancellation.


Deliver: forward useful objects
A relay can receive content once and forward it to several viewers. Each viewer has a separate connection, so one may build a queue while another keeps up. Priorities and delivery timeouts help decide which work to send and which to abandon. Relays and Distribution explains the paths; Latency and Congestion explains what happens when they slow down.


Present: turn objects into sound and pictures
The player interprets the media format, decodes the content, and schedules playback. Receiving bytes is only part of that work: the player also needs a usable decoding starting point and timestamps. Media and the Browser follows the path from received objects to the screen and speakers.

How do the layers fit together?
These activities involve several layers of software. The application knows about the lecture and its viewers. The media format describes the audio and video. MOQT delivers named content, and the transport underneath carries the bytes.

Suppose the viewer connects successfully but sees no picture. The connection may be working while the application requests the wrong track. Or objects may arrive correctly while the player lacks the information to decode them. Each layer gives us a separate question to investigate. We will learn the layers individually, then follow content through the whole system.

title: 1  What, Why and How
section: How does MoQ compare with WebRTC?
text:
How does MoQ compare with WebRTC?
WebRTC and MoQ can both carry a live conversation or a broadcast. They organize the work differently. WebRTC gives a browser an integrated media connection; MOQT gives applications a way to publish and request named content. The practical difference is how much of the media system your chosen stack supplies.

What the browser does for you
For a video call, the browser’s WebRTC stack handles encoding, media transport, receiving, and decoding. The application uses RTCPeerConnection, supplies signaling to exchange setup information, and decides who joins the room. Capturing a microphone and attaching received media to a player still require application code. See the WebRTC API.
MOQT itself supplies no camera API, codec, or player. It delivers objects. A MoQ media library must describe those objects, encode and decode media, and arrange playback. The library can hide much of this work, but its capabilities are separate from what the transport specification guarantees. That separation lets a relay forward the same named content without understanding its codec. See the MOQT object model.


How content reaches people
WebRTC uses ICE to find a working path between endpoints. STUN helps discover reachable addresses; TURN supplies a relay path when needed. In a group call, a selective forwarding unit, or SFU, can receive each participant’s media and forward selected streams to others. An SFU handles media distribution; a TURN server relays traffic along a connection path. These are different jobs. See RFC 8835 §3.4 and RFC 7667 §3.7.
A browser MoQ client normally opens an outgoing WebTransport connection to a server. MoQ relays distribute requested tracks and can retain objects for later requests. For our lecture, that means a relay can forward the current audio while supplying a newly arrived viewer with earlier video needed to begin decoding. Caching is an explicit part of MOQT’s relay model; retaining enough useful content remains an implementation decision.


Questions to ask when choosing an implementation

Neither protocol name tells you the final delay, operating cost, or audience limit. Those depend on the encoder, topology, buffering, available bandwidth, and software. QUIC’s streams help organize delivery, but they do not eliminate congestion. WebRTC’s integrated media stack does not restrict it to small calls. MoQ’s distribution model does not restrict it to broadcasts.


They can work together
An existing WebRTC publisher can feed a gateway that publishes the content over MoQ. The gateway has to translate media packaging and session behavior; replacing a socket is not enough. Lorenzo Miniero’s Meetecho interoperability demo shows one such bridge. That 2024 article uses older drafts, so use it to understand the architecture rather than today’s message formats.
For a practical evaluation, start with one complete path: a speaker, a relay or media server, and a viewer on a constrained connection. Measure join time, conversational delay, stalls, and recovery. Then increase the audience. Cloudflare’s account of its MoQ work explains the distribution motivation from an operator’s perspective; the webrtcHacks use-case comparison offers another author’s assessment of the tradeoffs. These are useful implementation perspectives, not performance guarantees from a standard.

title: 1  What, Why and How
text:
The protocol and the project
You will encounter two related names as you read: the IETF MoQ work and the moq.dev project. The IETF, the Internet Engineering Task Force, develops the transport specification through public drafts. moq.dev provides applications and libraries, including a smaller protocol model called moq-lite and a media format called hang.
This book uses MOQT draft-21, published September 8, 2026, as its IETF baseline. It is an Internet-Draft, still being developed rather than a finished RFC. The moq.dev examples describe project documentation reviewed on September 16, 2026. We identify implementation-specific behavior as we encounter it, so you can tell which ideas belong to the transport specification and which belong to the example software. When connecting implementations, check that their protocol revisions and media formats agree.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
A short introduction to TCP/IP
QUIC carries application data over a secure connection with multiple independent byte streams. WebTransport gives browser applications access to streams and datagrams. Understanding these tools explains what MOQT can ask the transport to do when data is delayed or lost.
We will start with the TCP/IP basics, then examine stream ordering, loss, cancellation, and datagrams. Next we will connect those ideas to security and the browser’s WebTransport interface. The final section looks inside QUIC packets and the handshake; you can return to that detail after learning the content model. You do not need to memorize packet headers to follow the book.
If you are already familiar with TCP/IP, TCP, and UDP, skip ahead to Why one ordered stream can hurt.
The Internet connects networks. A router forwards packets toward a destination, usually through other routers. IP, the Internet Protocol, supplies addressing and packet delivery across those networks. An IP address identifies a network interface; it is not a permanent identity for a person or an application.
A packet contains a header, which describes how to handle it, and a payload, the data it carries. Layers nest: the payload of an IP packet can contain a UDP datagram, whose payload contains QUIC packets. The receiving software unwraps those layers.
An address gets traffic to a host. A port helps the host direct that traffic to the appropriate transport endpoint. A server may listen for QUIC on UDP port 443 while serving TCP connections on TCP port 443: the transport protocol is part of the distinction. DNS translates a name such as relay.example into addresses the client can try. DNS resolution alone does not establish a connection.
IP delivery is best effort. Packets can be lost, duplicated, reordered, or delayed. A full queue in a router is one reason for loss. Each link has a maximum transmission unit, or MTU: its largest IP packet size. The path MTU is the smallest link MTU along the route. Sending one large application message does not make the network carry it as one arbitrarily large packet. See the IPv6 specification for packet-size constraints.

TCP and UDP make different promises
TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, provides an ordered byte stream. It tracks bytes, acknowledges progress, and repairs loss. The application reads a continuous sequence rather than individual network packets. If the connection fails, reliable delivery does not make the missing bytes magically arrive.
UDP, the User Datagram Protocol, preserves message boundaries but does not supply ordering or retransmission. The application receives individual datagrams that reach it. A protocol built above UDP can add reliability, security, and congestion control. QUIC does exactly that.

The comparison concerns the transport service, not a speed ranking. A UDP application still needs responsible sending behavior. A TCP application can have low latency. QUIC offers a different way to organize delivery. The base specifications are TCP, RFC 9293, UDP, RFC 768, and QUIC, RFC 9000.


Delay, rate, and feedback
Bandwidth describes a path’s carrying capacity. Throughput is the rate actually achieved. Latency is delay; always name the interval being measured. Network delay and the delay from a camera capturing a picture to a screen displaying it are different measurements.
An acknowledgment, or ACK, tells a sender what transport data arrived. Round-trip time, or RTT, measures a trip to the peer and back. A sender uses feedback to estimate the path and detect possible loss. An ACK does not prove that a video decoder accepted the bytes or that a viewer saw the picture.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
section: Why one ordered stream can hurt
text:
Why one ordered stream can hurt
Imagine sending camera video and captions through a single ordered byte stream. A packet containing video bytes goes missing. Later caption bytes arrive, but the receiver cannot expose them through that stream until the missing earlier bytes are recovered. This is head-of-line blocking.
Ordering is often exactly what we want. The trouble is imposing one ordering on unrelated work. Captions may be useful even while an old video frame is being repaired.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
Independent streams
QUIC provides multiple reliable, ordered byte streams within one connection. Loss affecting one stream does not impose that stream’s delivery order on another. A stream still has its own ordering: later bytes in that same stream wait for missing earlier bytes.
A byte stream has no built-in message boundaries. If the publisher writes two objects, the receiver cannot assume two reads will return those two objects. MOQT supplies framing so the receiver can find where each object starts and ends. RFC 9000 §2.2 explains this distinction.
The independence is not unlimited. Streams still compete for connection bandwidth, and connection-level flow control can constrain them together. QUIC removes a particular delivery dependency; it does not give every stream a private network.
QUIC applies flow-control limits to both individual streams and their combined data. A receiver that stops consuming one stream can therefore hold up other streams if the connection-wide limit is exhausted. See RFC 9000 §4.1 and RFC 9002 §7.
MoQ takes advantage of this distinction by putting independently useful content on different streams. The grouping decisions above the transport determine how useful that independence becomes.

Suppose camera bytes use stream A and captions use stream B. The offsets below are illustrative byte positions, not MoQ object IDs.

This is the benefit of separate stream ordering. If the lost packet had carried data from both streams, both could have gaps. Congestion feedback can also slow the whole connection. Stream independence does not mean immunity to the same network failure.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
Reliability can have an ending
Reliable delivery means lost stream bytes can be retransmitted. It does not mean the application must keep a stream alive forever. A sender can reset a stream; a receiver can ask it to stop. That gives a live application a way to abandon work.
Consider an old camera group that is still incomplete when a fresh independent group becomes available. Continuing to repair the old group may improve completeness, but delay the picture the viewer wants now. Cancelling old work is an application decision enabled by the transport.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
Where datagrams fit
QUIC’s DATAGRAM extension provides messages that are not retransmitted by QUIC when lost. They share the connection’s security and congestion control. They do not promise arrival or ordering, and their size is constrained by the path and negotiated limits.
QUIC does not split a DATAGRAM frame across packets. If an application’s message is too large, it must choose another mapping or define its own fragmentation and reassembly. That also means deciding what to do when one fragment is missing. See RFC 9221 §5.
That can suit a small, replaceable sensor update. It is less convenient for a large video frame that cannot fit in a datagram. A protocol must define how content maps onto these tools; “uses UDP” alone says very little about reliability.
A QUIC datagram is also different from a UDP packet. QUIC adds its own framing, encryption, and congestion behavior on top of UDP.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
Security belongs to the connection
Running over UDP does not mean sending plaintext. QUIC uses Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3, the security protocol also used by HTTPS, to authenticate the server and establish keys that protect packets. With a relay in the middle, the publisher-to-relay and relay-to-viewer connections have separate protection. Hiding the content from the relay itself requires another layer, which we will discuss in the security chapter. See RFC 9001 §4.

text:
WebTransport is the browser doorway
Browser JavaScript does not generally get a raw QUIC socket. WebTransport exposes streams and datagrams to web applications. For the MOQT mapping described in this edition, the browser uses WebTransport over HTTP/3; native software can use QUIC directly.

WebTransport transports application bytes. It does not know that those bytes represent a subscription, an Opus packet, or a camera frame. A MoQ implementation still has to implement the protocol above it.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
A fallback changes the tradeoffs
The moq.dev stack documents a WebSocket fallback. This can help reach networks where the preferred transport is unavailable. It does not preserve all of QUIC’s independent-stream behavior: TCP provides one reliable, ordered byte stream. When the fallback carries all its work over that stream, missing bytes can hold up later bytes belonging to unrelated work.
When testing a player, record which transport it actually used. Otherwise, you can spend a long time explaining “QUIC performance” while measuring a different path.
For a first mental model, keep three questions separate: can the client connect, can the peers speak the same MoQ version, and can the receiver use the content? Each can fail while the previous one succeeds.

text:
Reading a QUIC packet
The rest of this chapter looks inside the transport. You can continue to Tracks, Groups and Objects now and return here when you want to read packet fields.
A QUIC frame is a transport instruction inside a QUIC packet. It is unrelated to a video frame, which represents a picture. A packet can carry several QUIC frames, including stream data from different streams.

This is a reading guide, not a complete wire-format table. Field encodings and permitted frame combinations are defined in RFC 9000 §19; DATAGRAM is defined separately in RFC 9221.
Three numbers answer different questions: a packet number identifies a transmission within its packet-number space; a stream ID identifies a stream; a byte offset locates data within that stream. When lost stream data is sent again, it travels in a new packet, with a new packet number. It retains its position in the stream. See RFC 9000 §13.3 for how QUIC retransmits information.

title: 3  Tracks, Groups and Objects
text:
What is a track?
MoQ names content so that a viewer can request just the pieces it needs. In our lecture, a student joining late might want audio and low-resolution video without downloading the earlier ten minutes.
The content model has three levels: a track is a named sequence of groups, a group contains objects, and an object identifies one piece of data. We will work through those levels in order, then explain how subgroups organize delivery on streams. Finally, we will see why names must remain consistent after a publisher restarts and how moq-lite’s vocabulary differs.
A track is a named sequence of groups that a subscriber can request. Our lecture has separate tracks for audio, low-resolution video, and high-resolution video. Subscribing to video-low asks for that sequence; it does not also request video-high.
Tracks belong to a namespace, which lets the application organize related names. For this lecture, we use the namespace lectures / session-7. Together, the namespace and track name identify the full track.
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Selecting tracks from a lecture
  accDescr: The lecture namespace contains audio, video-low, and video-high tracks. The example viewer subscribes to audio and video-low.
  L["Namespace: lectures / session-7"] --> A["Track: audio"]
  L --> V["Track: video-low"]
  L --> H["Track: video-high"]
  A --> S["Student receives audio and low-resolution video"]
  V --> S
These readable labels are examples. On the wire, MOQT represents namespace components and track names as byte sequences. Both ends must agree on those bytes; writing the same-looking path in a user interface is not enough. See track naming in draft-21 §2.4.1.

title: 3  Tracks, Groups and Objects
section: How do groups provide starting points?
text:
How do groups provide starting points?
A group organizes objects within a track. A video format can use each group as a place to begin decoding. That answers the late-arriving student’s next question: where should playback start?
Many compressed pictures describe changes from earlier pictures. Receiving one of these predicted frames without its reference pictures is like receiving “move it two pixels to the left” without knowing what “it” is. A keyframe provides a picture from which decoding can restart.
For our video format, the publisher begins each group with a keyframe, then puts the frames that depend on it in the same group. The student can start with a recent group instead of reconstructing the entire lecture. The player also needs the codec configuration, which the media format supplies separately.

  accTitle: Two independently decodable video groups
  accDescr: Group 41 starts with its own keyframe and dependent frames. Group 42 starts with a new keyframe and has no picture dependency on group 41 in this example.
  subgraph G41["Group 41"]
    direction TB
    A["Object 0: keyframe"] --> B["Object 1: predicted frame"]
    B --> C["Object 2: predicted frame"]
  end
  subgraph G42["Group 42"]
    direction TB
    D["Object 0: new keyframe"] --> E["Object 1: predicted frame"]
    E --> F["Object 2: predicted frame"]
  end






Each arrow runs from a reference picture to a picture that needs it. These are decoding dependencies, not network packets. A viewer who has missed group 41 can still use group 42. This is why MOQT recommends independently useful groups. A group boundary alone cannot make a picture decodable: the publisher must put a suitable picture there.
Group IDs order groups within the track. Group 42 does not mean “42 seconds,” and groups need not have equal duration. The media format carries timing information for playback.

title: 3  Tracks, Groups and Objects
text:
What identifies an object?
Inside each group are objects. Each object has an ID and a payload: the bytes being delivered. Our example puts one encoded picture in each object. Other media formats can divide their data differently.

The identity applies within an agreed scope: the set of servers that treat a full track name as the same track. An unrelated service can use the same labels for different content. Within our lecture service’s scope, however, that complete identity must consistently refer to the same payload. See objects (§2.1) and scope (§2.5).
This property is called immutability. Once published, an object’s payload does not change. If Alice and Bob request the same object, a relay can serve the same stored bytes to both. A corrected payload needs a new identity; otherwise the relay would have no way to know which version the name means.

title: 3  Tracks, Groups and Objects
section: How do subgroups map objects to streams?
text:
How do subgroups map objects to streams?
A subgroup organizes objects from one group for delivery. It lets the publisher put related objects on the same stream while separating other work.
For subscription delivery, MOQT normally carries each subgroup on one subgroup stream. Within a subgroup, objects are ordered by object ID. This lets the publisher separate work that benefits from separate transport streams. A subgroup can use another stream if an earlier stream was reset prematurely or upstream conditions forced objects out of order; different subgroups must not share a subscription stream.
For example, a layered video codec might produce a base layer that gives a usable picture and an enhancement layer that adds detail. Putting them in separate subgroups lets a scheduler favor the base layer when capacity is scarce. The enhancement still depends on the base; a separate stream does not remove that media dependency.
A subgroup organizes delivery; its ID is not an extra component of the object address in the table above. Objects delivered as datagrams do not belong to subgroups, and fetched objects have their own stream representation. These distinctions are defined in draft-21 §2.2.

Keep the two kinds of structure separate
A track describes content. A stream carries bytes. Their lifetimes need not match: one video track can continue throughout the lecture while new subgroup streams open as new groups are published.

Separating these questions avoids a common mistake: opening a new transport stream does not create a new video track or a new decoding starting point.

title: 3  Tracks, Groups and Objects
section: What happens to names after a restart?
text:
What happens to names after a restart?
Suppose the lecturer’s publisher crashes. When it restarts, it reuses video-low, group 42, object 1 for a new picture. A relay still has the old picture stored under that address. It cannot safely treat both as the same immutable object.
One solution is to give the restarted publication a fresh namespace, such as lectures / session-8. Another is to preserve a non-conflicting sequence of group IDs. The application must choose a strategy that keeps old and new identities distinct throughout its scope.
The same naming rules that make caching useful make this restart decision necessary. In the next chapter, we will follow a request for one of these named tracks from the student to the publisher.

title: 3  Tracks, Groups and Objects
section: How does moq-lite name these concepts?
text:
How does moq-lite name these concepts?
When working with the moq-lite implementation, you will encounter broadcast for a named collection of tracks and frame for the payload unit corresponding to an object. moq-lite omits MOQT subgroups and uses a simpler group-per-stream model. Keep that distinction in mind when moving between its documentation and the IETF specification.

title: 4  Publishing and Subscribing
text:
Establishing a session
A subscription asks another endpoint to deliver objects from a named track. It connects the content model from the previous chapter to the actual exchange between a publisher and a subscriber.
We will follow Alice, a student joining the lecture, through five parts of that exchange: establishing a session, finding the lecture, requesting audio, joining video in the middle, and ending a subscription. The examples show which endpoint sends each message and what its response establishes. Setup and delivery can overlap; the order of the explanation is not a requirement to wait after every step.
Before Alice and the relay can exchange requests, they need a compatible MoQ session. A session is the protocol relationship in which the endpoints exchange requests and content. The transport carries that conversation, but it does not interpret its messages.
In MOQT draft-21, version selection happens during transport establishment. Native QUIC uses ALPN, a handshake field identifying the application protocol; WebTransport uses its protocol negotiation header. The identifier for this edition’s draft is moqt-21. This is why a working network path is only part of establishing a connection: the endpoints must also agree on the protocol they will speak. See §6.2.
Each endpoint opens a control stream and starts it with SETUP, exchanging session options and supported extensions. Each control stream is unidirectional: only the endpoint that opened it sends on it. A request such as SUBSCRIBE uses a separate bidirectional stream, so the other endpoint can answer on that same stream. Objects travel separately from these request messages.
The implementation can overlap some of this work. Requests and data may be sent while initialization is still underway. The draft recommends buffering early arrivals until setup completes, but permits an endpoint to reset early request streams if it cannot support or does not want to buffer them. The separate steps explain their responsibilities, rather than imposing a round trip for each one. See §6.3.

From a connection to the first object

Discovery is omitted because this client already knows the track name. SUBSCRIBE_OK accepts a request; it does not mean the first picture has been decoded. The separate streams are specified in draft-21 §6.4.

title: 4  Publishing and Subscribing
text:
Finding the lecture
Before asking for media, the application must turn Alice’s choice into track names. The lecture page might already contain a publication name, or it might use namespace discovery to find available publishers. Discovery supplies information about what is available within the service; the application decides how to present that information as a room list, an invitation, or a public directory.
Once it finds the publication, the player reads its media description. This tells it which tracks contain audio and which contain video renditions: alternative encodings, such as low-resolution and high-resolution video. Alice’s player can start by choosing audio and a low-resolution rendition. We will examine that media description in the browser chapter.
Discovery and delivery can have different access rules. A private lecture might be hidden from the room list as well as unavailable for playback. Knowing its name does not grant permission to receive it. MOQT provides namespace discovery mechanisms; the service supplies the access policy.

title: 4  Publishing and Subscribing
text:
Asking for audio
Alice’s player sends SUBSCRIBE, naming the lecture’s audio track and specifying its delivery choices. The relay answers with SUBSCRIBE_OK if it accepts, or REQUEST_ERROR if it rejects the request. Acceptance establishes the subscription. Audio objects arrive separately from the request and response messages.
Suppose the relay is not yet receiving this lecture. The service has associated the publication with an upstream publisher through registration, routing configuration, or implementation-specific discovery. The relay uses that information to make an upstream subscription of its own; a track name is not an Internet-wide lookup service. The following example begins after setup and shows one possible sequence. Both subscriptions request compatible delivery settings.





sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: A viewer subscribes through a relay
    accDescr: Alice subscribes to audio at the relay. The relay obtains an upstream subscription from the publisher, accepts Alice's request, and forwards audio objects.
    participant A as Alice
    participant R as Relay
    participant P as Publisher
    A->>R: SUBSCRIBE audio
    R->>P: SUBSCRIBE audio
    P-->>R: SUBSCRIBE_OK
    R-->>A: SUBSCRIBE_OK
    P->>R: Audio objects
    R->>A: Audio objects






Alice’s subscription and the relay’s upstream subscription belong to different sessions. The relay receives objects as a subscriber, then supplies them to Alice as a publisher. It may already have an upstream subscription or cached content, so every new viewer need not cause this whole exchange.
Now Bob opens the same lecture and asks for the same audio. The relay can reuse its upstream content while maintaining a separate downstream subscription for Bob. If Alice leaves, Bob still needs that content. If both leave, and no recorder or other consumer remains, the relay can cancel its upstream request. This is how a relay combines demand without making every viewer share one connection. See §7.
The publisher can initiate a subscription too, by offering a track with PUBLISH. The receiver accepts with REQUEST_OK—called PUBLISH_OK when accepting a publication in this draft—or rejects with REQUEST_ERROR. A relay must already know the client is interested in and authorized for that content. Either direction of initiation establishes the same kind of subscription. See §3.1.

title: 4  Publishing and Subscribing
text:
Joining video in the middle
Audio is arriving, and Alice’s player also requests video. The publisher is halfway through group 42. In our example, the group’s first object contains a keyframe and the later frames depend on earlier pictures. Receiving only the next new frame may therefore leave Alice with bytes she cannot decode.
The player can retrieve the beginning of group 42 while following new objects, or wait for the next independent group. The first choice can start playback sooner if the missing content is available and quick to deliver. The second avoids catching up through the current group, but waits for a new decoding starting point.
A fetch requests a bounded portion of a track. In draft-21, a standalone FETCH receives FETCH_OK or REQUEST_ERROR; fetched objects use a separate data stream. Successful delivery finishes when that data stream ends. Acceptance tells the requester that its request was accepted, rather than that every object has already arrived. See §3.2.1.
For Alice’s first choice, draft-21 also allows FILL_PARAMETERS on the subscription. These request a bounded fill range on a fetch stream alongside ongoing subscription delivery. The ranges can overlap, so the player must handle duplicate objects; pairing a fill through the largest known object with a subscription starting at the next object avoids that overlap. For the second choice, a location filter can start delivery at the next group. A location is a group ID and object ID: a position in the track, rather than a clock reading. See fill ranges (§3.4) and location filters (§3.3.1).





flowchart TD
    accTitle: Two ways to join a video track
    accDescr: Alice joins during group 42. She can retrieve its earlier objects and follow new ones, or wait for the independently decodable group 43. Either route needs codec configuration before decoding.
    J["Alice joins during group 42"] --> C["Retrieve earlier objects in group 42"]
    J --> W["Wait for group 43"]
    C --> F["Combine with ongoing delivery"]
    W --> K["Receive group 43 from its keyframe"]
    F --> D["Decode with the codec configuration"]
    K --> D






Filling the current group uses retained data; starting with the next group waits for new data. Neither route can promise an immediate picture. Retained objects take time to transfer, and the next keyframe may not have been produced yet.
Both choices depend on the media format identifying usable starting points. Switching from low-resolution to high-resolution video raises the same question: where can the decoder begin using the new rendition?
Fetching also depends on retention. The relay may have discarded the beginning of group 42, or never received it. To offer a “rewind 30 seconds” button, the service must retain enough content and map playback time to track locations. The fetch mechanism provides a way to request that content; storage and timing information make the feature possible.

title: 4  Publishing and Subscribing
text:
Ending a subscription
When Alice disables video, her player should cancel the video subscription while leaving audio active. Otherwise, the relay continues doing work she no longer needs.
In draft-21, cancellation abruptly closes the request stream’s open directions. STOP_SENDING asks the peer to stop its sending direction; RESET_STREAM abandons the cancelling endpoint’s own sending direction. A plain FIN only means that no more bytes will be sent in one direction. A subscriber can finish sending request messages while still expecting content, so FIN alone does not cancel the request. See §6.4.2.2–3.
When the publisher ends an established subscription, it closes the associated data streams, sends PUBLISH_DONE, and closes its request-stream direction. The data streams and request stream can arrive in different orders. Alice may therefore receive PUBLISH_DONE while some final object data is still on its way. See §3.1.1 and §9.9.
Subscription lifetime also matters to authorization. If Alice’s permission expires during the lecture, the service needs a policy for the subscription she already holds, as well as for any new request. Publication permission is separate: allowing Alice to watch must not allow her to replace the lecturer’s content.

title: 5  Relays and Distribution
text:
How does a relay share content?
A relay receives content from a publisher and forwards it to subscribers. It moves the copying work off the publisher’s connection, allowing the same publication to reach more viewers.
This chapter follows that work in four parts: sharing upstream content, interpreting the metadata needed to forward it, caching objects for later requests, and adapting delivery to each downstream connection. We will finish by separating those jobs from transcoding and deployment choices. You will be able to trace where copies, stored objects, and queues exist in a distribution path.
A relay is a subscriber toward an upstream source and a publisher toward downstream subscribers. It terminates transport connections and handles MoQ metadata. It is more than a router forwarding encrypted IP packets.

With several interested viewers, a relay can share upstream content and forward it to each downstream connection. If a second relay is closer to another audience, it can repeat that pattern. A network of these relationships provides distribution across regions.
Each downstream connection still needs its own bytes. For one 2 Mb/s track and 100 viewers, the difference looks like this. These figures count payload only, before transport overhead.

title: 5  Relays and Distribution
section: What does a relay need to know?
text:
What does a relay need to know?
A relay uses names, group boundaries, priorities, and delivery rules. It need not inspect the encoded picture to forward it. That separation makes a generic relay useful for audio, video, and application data.
The publisher must therefore align the group boundaries with the media. If a group advertised as a starting point depends on an earlier group, forwarding it will not give the new viewer enough information to decode. Format design and encoder behavior must agree.

title: 5  Relays and Distribution
section: How does caching help new viewers?
text:
How does caching help new viewers?
A caching relay can hold recently received objects. A new viewer may obtain a useful group without waiting for the original publisher to send it again. An object is identified by its full track name, group ID, and object ID within a scope. Its payload cannot change, allowing different viewers to reuse the same cached bytes. Some object properties can change under their own rules; immutability does not apply to every cached field.
MOQT permits caching; it does not require every relay to store every object. Even a caching relay has a retention policy and finite memory. An accepted live subscription therefore tells the viewer nothing about how much history the relay retains.
For the lecture, retaining a few useful recent groups may improve startup. Keeping the entire class for replay is a separate storage feature with different costs and lifetime requirements.

title: 5  Relays and Distribution
section: How does delivery differ between viewers?
text:
How does delivery differ between viewers?
The lecturer’s connection can be fast while one viewer’s connection is slow. A relay has to make downstream delivery decisions for each path. Slowing every viewer to match the slowest one would defeat the point of independent subscriptions.
Alice’s connection may deliver each new group immediately, while Bob’s connection builds a queue. Their playback delay differs even though both request the same publication. The relay can choose delivery settings for each subscription according to that viewer’s path.
Measure at the edges, then trace through the hops. A healthy publisher-to-relay connection says little about a congested relay-to-viewer connection.

title: 5  Relays and Distribution
section: Which jobs belong to the wider service?
text:
Which jobs belong to the wider service?
Forwarding a high-resolution track does not create a low-resolution version. A transcoder decodes and re-encodes media; a relay distributes the objects it receives. A service can run both roles, but they are different jobs.
Likewise, DNS routing, selecting a nearby relay, arranging redundancy, and recovering application state are deployment choices. The moq.dev project supplies clustering features; they should not be mistaken for a universal, automatic global MoQ network.
Before scaling the lecture, draw the actual publisher, relay, and viewer paths. Mark where content is cached and where authorization is checked. That small drawing often reveals more than a single “CDN” box.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
text:
Which rates and delays are we measuring?
Playback latency is the time between capturing media and presenting it to a viewer. Some of that time is spent processing and moving data; some is spent waiting in queues. A connection can keep delivering objects while the viewer falls seconds behind.
We will first establish the units and account for that delay. Then we will follow a growing queue, distinguish congestion control from media adaptation, and examine priorities and delivery timeouts. Finally, we will look at the player’s own queue and how it returns to live playback. The numerical examples are teaching values, not benchmarks.
A bit is a binary digit; a byte contains eight bits. Network rates commonly use bits per second, while file sizes commonly use bytes. Here, the prefixes are decimal: one megabit is one million bits.
A connection can have high capacity and a long delay. “Fast” is ambiguous; use the rate or time that explains the problem. Transport overhead also consumes capacity, so media bitrate and network bitrate are not identical.

text:
Where does playback delay come from?
Capture-to-display latency includes capture, encoding, network transit, buffering, decoding, and presentation. A relay or operating system can add another queue along the way. Measuring only the network leaves much of the path unexplained.
Consider this illustrative budget for one frame. The numbers are teaching values, not a MoQ benchmark.

The appropriate balance depends on the interaction. Someone listening to a lecture may accept additional buffering to avoid interruptions. Someone speaking with the lecturer needs responses quickly and may prefer occasional missing video to a growing conversational delay.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
section: Why does the queue keep growing?
text:
Why does the queue keep growing?
Suppose the publisher produces four megabits each second while Alice’s path carries two. Each second adds two megabits to a queue. After five seconds, ten megabits are waiting, ignoring overhead. Even if production stops at that moment, sending that backlog at two megabits per second takes another five seconds.
If production continues at the same rate, waiting longer makes the problem worse. The application must reduce future work, abandon some queued work, or accept increasing delay. This arithmetic applies whether the transport is MoQ, WebRTC, or something else.
Congestion control limits what the transport sends to avoid overwhelming the network. The transport adjusts its sending rate in response to congestion signals; it does not directly know the path’s available capacity. That protects the path, but it cannot decide whether Alice would prefer a smaller picture or an old high-resolution one. That is the job of media adaptation. See RFC 9002 §7.
The player might request a lower-bitrate rendition, or the publisher might reduce future encoding quality. Reducing production below the rate the path can carry stops further queue growth. Existing queued data still has to be delivered or abandoned. To return near the live edge, the system may also need to skip old content.

Congestion control, flow control, and adaptation
Three mechanisms influence how much data is sent. They solve different problems:








Mechanism
Question it answers
Example




QUIC congestion control
How much traffic can this network path carry?
Packet loss causes the sender to reduce its sending rate


QUIC flow control
How much stream data is the receiver willing to accept?
The receiver stops granting more credit while its buffers are full


Media adaptation
How much media should the application produce or request?
The player switches from a 4 Mb/s rendition to a 1 Mb/s rendition



Flow control protects the receiver with limits on individual streams and the connection as a whole. It does not measure whether a frame is still worth displaying. See RFC 9000 §4. A player can therefore receive data reliably and within its allowed limits while still falling behind the lecture.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
section: How do priorities choose what to send?
text:
How do priorities choose what to send?
Before discarding content, the sender can choose how to divide the available capacity. In our lecture, preserving audio while reducing video may let Alice continue following the explanation. A scheduler—the part of the implementation choosing which pending data to send—needs to know that preference.
MOQT represents these preferences through priorities and group ordering. In draft-21, a lower numeric priority means more urgent work. The recommended scheduler considers subscriber priority before publisher priority. Within the same subscription, group ordering helps choose among groups when those priorities are equal. This is a recommendation, not a guarantee of one scheduling algorithm in every implementation. The full scheduling rules are in §5.1.
Priority changes which work waits. It does not reserve bandwidth or guarantee arrival by a deadline. If urgent audio consumes the available capacity, less urgent video may remain queued. That is why scheduling preferences need to be paired with limits on how long old work remains useful. Check the conventions of the API you use: moq-lite and MOQT fields are not interchangeable merely because both are called priorities.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
text:
When should delivery stop?
Suppose video group 41 remains incomplete while group 42 provides a fresh decoding starting point. Finishing group 41 would preserve older pictures, but sending group 42 may bring Alice closer to the lecturer. Independent groups make that choice possible without requiring every preceding picture.
The sender still has to respect the stream’s structure. A reliable byte stream cannot deliver later bytes past a missing section. To abandon a subgroup’s remaining stream data, MOQT resets that stream. A receiver must then use the media format’s dependencies to decide where decoding can resume.
Draft-21 defines two optional delivery timeouts. Their different starting points address different places where data can wait. The following examples use a relay’s local clock and a 100 ms timeout. They are separate examples, rather than two required stages for each object. See §5.2.

Waiting to enter the transport
The object delivery timeout measures age from when the last byte of an object’s header arrives from upstream. At the original publisher, it starts when the application supplies that header. Before handing the object to the underlying transport, the implementation checks its age.





flowchart TD
    accTitle: Object delivery timeout example
    accDescr: The relay receives the complete object header at zero milliseconds. At 120 milliseconds it checks whether to send the object. The 100 millisecond limit has passed, so it resets a subgroup stream or drops a datagram.
    A["0 ms: header received"] --> B["120 ms: ready to send"]
    B --> C["Age exceeds 100 ms"]
    C --> D["Subgroup: reset stream"]
    C --> E["Datagram: drop it"]






Here the object has already spent too long waiting before transmission. For a subgroup, expiry resets the stream rather than removing a few bytes from its middle. For a datagram, the expired message is dropped.
This check is most effective when the application can still control the queue. If it hands large amounts of data to the transport in advance, expired bytes may already be beyond its reach. Draft-21 therefore recommends minimizing transport buffering and checking expiry before retransmission where the transport interface permits it.


Waiting for delivery to finish
The subgroup delivery timeout starts when the endpoint knows all objects in the subgroup have been published. At a relay, receiving the upstream stream’s FIN provides that information. This timer covers remaining delivery work, including recovery after packet loss.





flowchart TD
    accTitle: Subgroup delivery timeout example
    accDescr: At 50 milliseconds the relay learns the subgroup is complete and starts a 100 millisecond timer. At 150 milliseconds it resets the stream if transport delivery is still incomplete.
    A["50 ms: subgroup complete"] --> B["Start 100 ms timer"]
    B --> C["150 ms: still undelivered?"]
    C -->|Yes| D["Reset stream"]
    C -->|No| E["Delivery finished"]






The transport must reach what the specification calls “all data committed” before the timer expires: its completion state for delivering the data, beyond merely accepting bytes into a send buffer. This concerns transport delivery, not whether the player has decoded or displayed the media. Otherwise, the stream is reset. Unlike the object age check, this timer can expire after the sender has handed all the data to the transport.
For datagrams, the subgroup timeout instead uses the same age check as the object timeout; if both are nonzero, the smaller value applies. Zero disables the corresponding timeout. These rules describe a single hop’s delivery decisions. They do not create a capture-to-display deadline across the whole relay network.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
section: How does the player return to live?
text:
How does the player return to live?
After the network recovers, Alice may still be watching frames that reached her earlier. A fresh transport queue does not empty the player’s playback queue. The player needs its own policy for skipping stale decoded frames or moving its presentation clock forward, while respecting audio synchronization and decoding dependencies.
This gives us two places to observe recovery: when fresh objects arrive, and when fresh content is actually displayed. Measuring both distinguishes network backlog from playback backlog.
A useful experiment briefly reduces available bandwidth and then restores it. Watch whether playback returns near live, stays behind, or repeatedly changes rendition. Record interruptions as well as average delay. A large keyframe can briefly exceed the path’s capacity even when the average bitrate fits, so the sequence of events matters.
Use a repeatable recorded source for the first experiment. It keeps scene complexity and encoder load stable while you investigate the network response. Once you understand that run, repeat on real devices and networks, where capture, rendering, and additional queues can change the result.

title: 7  Media and the Browser
text:
How does the player interpret a track?
A player turns received objects into sound and pictures. MOQT delivers the objects; the media format and player tell the browser how to interpret, decode, and present them.
We will follow that path in order: read the media description, find a decodable starting point, submit encoded data to a decoder, and schedule the result for playback. The final section covers browser permissions and resource cleanup. Our examples use the moq.dev hang media layer and the browser’s WebCodecs API, both of which we will introduce below.
The lecture offers an audio track and two video tracks, one at a lower resolution for slower connections. Track names let the player request them, but names alone do not explain how to use their bytes. The player also needs the codec, decoder configuration, and timing information. A codec defines how pictures or sound are encoded and decoded. A container packages the encoded data with information needed to interpret it, such as timestamps.
MOQT carries application payloads without choosing their media format. Our example uses hang, the media layer in the moq.dev stack. Its catalog.json track describes the available renditions and their decoder configuration. A rendition is an alternative encoding of the content, such as the lecture’s lower-resolution picture. See the hang catalog and container documentation.
Suppose the selected video rendition contains H.264 pictures at 1280 × 720 pixels. Its codec identifier tells the player which decoder it needs. Its codec configuration supplies any required setup, either as initialization data or in-band as the format permits, and its container field tells the player how to find the encoded chunks and their timestamps. With this information, the player can check support on the student’s device and subscribe to a suitable track.
flowchart TD
    accTitle: From a lecture catalog to a displayed picture
    accDescr: The player reads the catalog, selects a supported rendition, receives its media objects, parses encoded chunks and timestamps, decodes pictures, then schedules and displays them.
    A[Read the media catalog] --> B[Choose a supported rendition]
    B --> C[Subscribe and receive objects]
    C --> D[Parse chunks and timestamps]
    D --> E[Decode pictures]
    E --> F[Schedule and display]
    A -. Decoder configuration .-> E
    D -. Media timestamps .-> F
The catalog remains useful after playback starts. The lecturer might add screen sharing, or a rendition might temporarily become unavailable. The player needs to respond to those updates instead of treating the initial list as permanent.

text:
Four things that are easy to confuse

Decoded frame

An encoded chunk is a unit of compressed media submitted to a decoder. The media format defines how these chunks fit into objects. MOQT itself does not require one object to equal one video frame. Keeping that boundary clear helps locate failures: receiving an object proves delivery, while displaying a picture also requires parsing, decoding, and scheduling.

title: 7  Media and the Browser
text:
Where can decoding begin?
Video compression often describes how one picture differs from earlier pictures. Such a predicted frame is useful only when the decoder has the reference pictures it needs. A keyframe supplies a fresh decoding starting point in the video model we are using.
This explains the group boundaries from the object-model chapter. The publisher starts a video group with a keyframe, then places dependent frames after it. Our late-arriving student can retrieve the beginning of the current group or wait for the next group. Receiving only the middle of a group may leave the decoder without its references, even though every requested byte arrived correctly.
The encoder and packager must agree on those boundaries. Cutting a stream every second does not itself create independent video sequences. The media format also has to supply the decoder configuration needed at the join point.
The same issue appears when the student switches to higher resolution. The new rendition has its own decoder state. The player changes configuration as needed and starts at a valid decoding point; it cannot simply feed an arbitrary high-resolution predicted frame into the old sequence.

title: 7  Media and the Browser
section: How does WebCodecs decode the media?
text:
How does WebCodecs decode the media?
WebCodecs gives JavaScript access to media encoders and decoders. For video, the player checks a configuration with VideoDecoder.isConfigSupported(), applies it with configure(), and submits encoded chunks with decode(). Support depends on the actual codec configuration and device, so the presence of the API alone is insufficient.
The decoder produces VideoFrame objects through an output callback. Those are decoded pictures ready for the next stage, rather than instructions to display immediately. The player owns the queues, presentation timing, and rendering. It also parses the incoming container before submitting chunks. These responsibilities explain why WebCodecs is a component of a player rather than a complete player. The VideoDecoder interface describes the API.
Each decoded frame holds resources. After rendering or discarding a frame, the player calls VideoFrame.close() when it no longer needs that frame. Waiting for garbage collection can retain scarce resources and stall decoding. Bounded queues are equally important: if rendering slows down, receiving more frames must not cause unlimited memory growth. See the WebCodecs memory model.

title: 7  Media and the Browser
section: When should a frame be presented?
text:
When should a frame be presented?
Frames do not necessarily arrive at the spacing at which they were captured. Variable network delay produces jitter. If the player displayed pictures on arrival, that uneven timing would become visible movement on the screen.
Media timestamps preserve the intended spacing. Consider these illustrative values, in milliseconds. The media timeline and receiver clock have different origins. These teaching values use milliseconds; WebCodecs VideoFrame.timestamp uses microseconds, so a player must convert units when mapping clocks.









Frame

The player chooses receiver time 160 as the moment to display media time zero. It adds each subsequent media timestamp to that anchor. Although B and C arrive only five milliseconds apart, the player displays them 34 milliseconds apart, preserving the media timeline.

Arrival time and presentation time





flowchart LR
    accTitle: Uneven arrivals become evenly scheduled presentation
    accDescr: Frame A arrives at receiver time 100 and is displayed at 160. B arrives at 145 and is displayed at 193. C arrives at 150 and is displayed at 227. Each frame waits until its scheduled display time.
    A["A arrives: 100 ms"] -->|"Wait 60 ms"| D["Display A: 160 ms"]
    B["B arrives: 145 ms"] -->|"Wait 48 ms"| E["Display B: 193 ms"]
    C["C arrives: 150 ms"] -->|"Wait 77 ms"| F["Display C: 227 ms"]






Each arrow follows one frame through the playback buffer. The diagram uses the table’s receiver clock; arrow lengths are not a time scale.
The initial wait gives later frames some room to arrive. If B instead arrives at receiver time 205, it misses its planned time of 193. The player must then apply its late-frame policy, perhaps skipping the picture or moving playback later. That is the buffering tradeoff: waiting longer can absorb more variation, at the cost of a later picture.


Keeping audio and video together
Audio follows the same presentation timeline. An audio sample and a picture intended for media time 67 ms can arrive separately; the player schedules them against a shared clock so the lecturer’s voice stays aligned with their face. Over longer sessions it may also need to correct differences between clocks.
Group and object IDs locate content; the media timestamps tell the player when to present it. Neither this table nor those IDs measure capture-to-display latency by themselves. That measurement also requires a relationship between the source’s capture clock and the receiver’s clock.

title: 7  Media and the Browser
section: What else does a browser player need?
text:
What else does a browser player need?
A student pressing Play brings the rest of the browser into the picture. Playback may require a user action under autoplay policy. A publisher capturing a camera or microphone needs capture permission; publishing a supplied file does not require access to those devices. See the media capture permission rules. Devices can disappear, tabs can become hidden, and the page must release resources when the session ends.
The moq.dev project provides higher-level player and publisher packages that handle much of this integration. Using its existing player gives a first experiment a working path through capture, decoding, and presentation. The chapter’s pipeline then provides a way to investigate a failure: determine whether the missing step is media discovery, a decodable starting point, decoding, or presentation.

title: 8  Security and Access
text:
What does the connection protect?
A secure connection protects traffic between its endpoints. A private lecture also needs rules about who may discover, watch, or publish it, and whether the relay operator may read its content.
This chapter separates those decisions. We will examine connection protection, participant permissions, and end-to-end content encryption, then apply them to cached content and resource limits. We will finish with tests for the access policy. The aim is to identify which part of the system enforces each rule.
QUIC uses TLS to establish packet-protection keys and authenticate the server. When a student’s browser verifies the relay’s certificate, it checks that it reached the expected relay under the applicable trust rules. That check does not identify the student to the relay. Client authentication is a separate choice, as explained in RFC 9001 §4.4.
The lecturer and student each have a connection to the relay. The relay terminates both, so it can read the application payload unless the application adds content encryption.
flowchart LR
    accTitle: Two protected connections through a relay
    accDescr: The lecturer connects securely to a relay, and the relay connects securely to the student. These are separate connections. The relay can read the media unless the application encrypts the content end to end.
    P[Lecturer] <-->|Protected connection A| R[Relay]
    R <-->|Protected connection B| S[Student]
For a service that trusts its relay operator with the lecture, this may be the intended arrangement. The transport protects traffic between endpoints, while the relay enforces access rules. A certificate failure should be corrected through the deployment’s trust configuration; disabling verification removes an essential check on which server receives the connection.

title: 8  Security and Access
section: Who may discover, subscribe, or publish?
text:
Who may discover, subscribe, or publish?
Authentication establishes identity. Authorization decides what that identity may do. In our lecture, the lecturer may publish under the class namespace, while students may subscribe to it. A student should not gain publication rights merely because they can watch.
First, write down the intended access policy. For example, this class might use:









Participant
Discover the class

Publish media

Yes

These are application rules, not built-in MOQT roles. Checking this table against actual requests is more useful than merely checking that every request has a token.
Access decisions extend to discovery. Even if an outsider cannot receive the objects, revealing a private lecture’s title may disclose information. The service should decide whether that outsider can discover the publication at all.
The application can carry these permissions in a credential, such as a JSON Web Token (JWT) where the implementation supports it. The relay must verify the credential and its restrictions: who issued it, which service it is for, whether it has expired, and which names and operations it permits. A token’s presence alone establishes none of these facts. RFC 8725 explains JWT validation, including checking the issuer and intended audience.
A stolen bearer credential can also be reused while it remains valid. Expiration limits its lifetime, but the deployment still needs a policy for stolen credentials and revocation. MOQT discusses this replay problem in draft-21 §15.3.2.

title: 8  Security and Access
section: How can content stay private from the relay?
text:
How can content stay private from the relay?
Some services need a stricter boundary: only the lecturer and enrolled students may read the content, including when a relay operator is untrusted. The lecturer then encrypts the media before handing it to the transport. Students decrypt it after receiving it. This is end-to-end content encryption.





flowchart LR
    accTitle: Content encryption across an intermediate relay
    accDescr: The lecturer encrypts media with content keys. The relay forwards the encrypted payload using visible routing metadata. An authorized student decrypts the media with the required content keys.
    P[Lecturer encrypts media] --> R[Relay forwards encrypted payload]
    R --> S[Student decrypts media]
    N[Names and delivery metadata remain visible] -.-> R






The service must distribute keys to authorized students, authenticate the content, decide when to change keys, and define how a newly enrolled student joins. These are part of the content-encryption design; establishing QUIC connections does not supply them automatically. MOQT leaves such mechanisms outside the transport specification. See draft-21 §15.4.
The relay can still route encrypted payloads using visible metadata. Names, sizes, timing, and subscription relationships can reveal information even when the lecture itself is unreadable. The trust decision therefore includes both who holds the content keys and what the forwarding service can observe.

title: 8  Security and Access
section: Who may publish under a cached name?
text:
Who may publish under a cached name?
The relay may retain objects so that another student can join quickly. This works because an object identity refers to the same payload wherever it is served within the service’s scope. If an attacker could publish different bytes under the lecturer’s identity, those bytes might reach several students through the cache.
Publication authorization must therefore establish ownership of the relevant names, as required by draft-21 §15.3.3. The service also needs to handle legitimate restarts: a lecturer who reconnects must not reuse old object identities for new payloads. A fresh publication namespace or a continuing non-conflicting sequence prevents old cached objects from colliding with new ones.

title: 8  Security and Access
section: How much work may a client request?
text:
How much work may a client request?
An enrolled student may be entitled to the lecture without being entitled to unlimited server resources. A client could subscribe to every rendition, repeatedly request discovery results, or leave streams stalled. Connections, subscriptions, queued bytes, and caches all consume resources that the service must bound.
Consider a low-priority video stream waiting while more urgent audio keeps arriving. Its bytes still occupy memory. In MOQT draft-21, each endpoint, whether publisher or subscriber, must cancel a stream when it reaches a resource limit, preferably its lowest-priority stream. The actual memory budget remains an implementation decision. See §15.5.
For the lecture service, a limit on concurrent track subscriptions can prevent one viewer from requesting every rendition while displaying only one. Monitoring those limits helps distinguish a slow student connection from an application that is creating more work than intended.

title: 8  Security and Access
section: How do we test the access policy?
text:
How do we test the access policy?
A successful playback test checks only the enrolled student’s path. Test the other roles too: a viewer attempting to publish, a student from another class attempting to subscribe, and a client beginning a request with an expired credential. Confirm that each fails at the intended boundary. Keep credentials out of copied logs and shared URLs wherever the integration permits.
For experiments, the moq.dev public anonymous relay is explicitly public and discoverable. Use public test content there. A private lecture needs a relay with deliberate access configuration, followed by the rejection tests above. The project’s development guide describes the public relay, and its production guide covers deployment access configuration.

title: 9  Your First MoQ System
text:
Choose and record the implementation
This walkthrough follows one publisher, one relay, and one viewer using the moq.dev local demo. The goal is to observe a complete media path and understand what each observation proves.
We will choose and record the implementation, review the path one frame takes, and start the demo with its supplied test content. Once playback works, we will add a second viewer, constrain the network, and consider what changes beyond localhost. The commands are upstream recipes, not a demo executed for this book.
This walkthrough uses the moq.dev project, including its moq-lite and hang stack. It is not a minimal implementation of every feature in MOQT draft-21. The project’s current documentation is the authority for installation and command changes.
Use its setup guide to install the prerequisites and obtain the project checkout. Record the checkout revision and library versions alongside your observations. A reproducible experiment needs more than the name “MoQ.”
The commands below are documented project recipes reviewed for this edition. They are meant to be run from the moq.dev repository, not from this book’s repository. They have not been executed as part of publishing this guide.

title: 9  Your First MoQ System
text:
Before running commands
A terminal lets you start programs by typing commands. Your working directory is the folder those commands run in. git clone downloads a repository; cd moq enters that checkout. git rev-parse HEAD prints its current commit identifier, which lets another reader locate the same source revision. Git’s revision documentation explains that command.
The demo runs several processes: running programs with separate jobs. A listener accepts traffic at an address and port. localhost refers to the machine running the client, so opening a localhost address on your phone does not connect to the demo on your laptop.
Keep the terminal running while using the demo. A process printing that it started is evidence about that process; it does not yet prove the browser can receive or play media.

title: 9  Your First MoQ System
section: Understand the path of one frame
text:
Understand the path of one frame
A source produces media. An encoder compresses it. The media layer supplies timing and configuration, and maps the encoded data into named tracks and groups. The publisher makes that content available through the relay.
The viewer chooses tracks, receives objects, interprets the media format, and decodes and presents the content. At each stage, ask what information is added and what can fail.
Your applicationRooms, permissions, playback decisionsMedia formatCodec configuration, timestamps, payloadsMoQ transportNames, subscriptions, groups, objectsQUIC / WebTransportSecure streams, datagrams, congestion controlEach layer solves a different problem. A working connection is only the beginning.
Once the demo is running, the observation table below will help you record the publication, transport, rendition, and codec.

Start with the local demo
This walkthrough follows the upstream quick start’s recommended Nix route, with flakes enabled. After installing that prerequisite, obtain the project and record the checkout you are using:

cd moq

The documented default recipe runs a local relay, a test publisher, and the web demo. Follow the setup guide if your platform needs additional configuration. Use the supplied test content first, so a camera permission failure cannot be mistaken for a transport failure.
Save the revision printed by git rev-parse HEAD with your notes. The final command, nix develop --command just, opens the development environment and starts the demo.

title: 9  Your First MoQ System
text:
Add a second viewer
Open another viewer for the same publication. The relay now has more downstream work, while the original publication can be shared upstream. Inspect the relay’s metrics or logs instead of assuming the bandwidth pattern from the diagram alone.
Then close one viewer. Confirm that the other continues. Close both and observe whether the chosen publisher stops producing or transmitting the unused track. Demand-aware behavior depends on the application path and other subscribers, so record what actually happens.

title: 9  Your First MoQ System
text:
Test a constrained network
Use a network test setup to constrain bandwidth or introduce delay. Start with one change at a time. Watch the selected rendition, playback age, audio continuity, and recovery after the constraint is removed.
Ordinary browser HTTP throttling tools may not shape every WebTransport path as expected. Verify that your chosen test tool affects the actual transport before drawing conclusions. Keep an unthrottled run as a baseline.
You are looking for understandable behavior: a lower rendition, a skipped group, a brief pause, or a growing backlog. “It stuttered” is a starting observation, not a diagnosis.

title: 9  Your First MoQ System
text:
Going beyond localhost
Moving to another machine adds certificate trust, network reachability, and access policy. QUIC uses UDP; opening only a TCP listener does not establish its path. Follow the deployment guide for the listener and fallback configuration actually in use.
Do not add recording, multiple regions, and private user accounts simultaneously. Add one boundary, verify it, then continue. When something breaks, the debugging chapter gives you a way to locate the first failed layer.
