title: 10  Debugging
text:
The transport never connects
Debugging a MoQ system means finding where progress stops between the publisher and the player. A black screen can result from a connection failure, a missing track, unusable media, or a presentation problem.
Start at the top of the path below and check each boundary until you reach the first missing fact. The sections follow that order, then address playback that falls behind. A worked frozen-video example shows how to turn observations into a test, followed by the evidence to collect for a bug report.
For example, if objects arrive but the decoder produces no frames, changing the relay address is unlikely to help. Start with the media format and decoder configuration. If decoded frames exist but the screen stays black, investigate presentation instead.
Check the endpoint address, certificate trust, listener, and network path. For a QUIC path, confirm UDP reachability. A successful HTTPS request to the same hostname may only prove TCP reachability.
If the application uses a fallback, log which transport won. Test from outside the server’s local network before concluding that a public endpoint works. Separate a certificate error from a timeout; their remedies are different.

title: 10  Debugging
section: The session opens, but nothing appears
text:
The session opens, but nothing appears
Confirm protocol compatibility and the scope or path the client joined. Then verify that the publication actually exists and the client is authorized to discover it. A connected client looking in the wrong namespace can wait forever without any packet loss.
Check the exact name bytes when working close to MOQT. Similar-looking text is not necessarily the same identifier. At the library level, inspect any normalization or path-prefix rules.

title: 10  Debugging
section: The track is found, but objects do not arrive
text:
The track is found, but objects do not arrive
Look for subscription acceptance or a specific rejection. Confirm the publisher is producing the requested track and the relay has an upstream source. Discovery of a publication is not proof that every expected track is available.
Keep the scope of an error with its code. In MOQT draft-21, a session error closes the protocol relationship, a REQUEST_ERROR rejects a particular request, and a stream reset ends that stream. For example, a DELIVERY_TIMEOUT stream reset does not by itself say that every other track stopped. A numeric code without its message or stream context is ambiguous because the error tables are separate. See draft-21 §12; moq-lite implementations may expose different errors.
Check filters, cancellation, and request lifetime. An accidentally closed subscription can look like a stalled network. If objects are requested from history, verify they remain retained; live availability does not imply old-object availability.

title: 10  Debugging
section: Objects arrive, but media does not play
text:
Objects arrive, but media does not play
Inspect the catalog, selected codec, decoder configuration, and the first usable decoding point. Starting with a predicted frame whose references are missing can fail even when delivery is perfect.
Then inspect decoding and presentation separately. Are decoded frames being produced? Is audio blocked by playback policy? Is the renderer waiting on a timestamp far in the future? Does a hidden tab change the scheduling behavior?
Use a known supported fixture to narrow the problem. If that works while one live source fails, examine the encoder and packaging before changing transport settings.

title: 10  Debugging
section: Playback works, but keeps falling behind
text:
Playback works, but keeps falling behind
Measure age and queue depth over time. Compare the source bitrate with achieved throughput. If the publisher persistently produces more than the path can carry, identify the adaptation or abandonment decision that should reduce the backlog.
A single average bitrate can hide bursts. A large keyframe can create a temporary queue even when the long-term average fits. Observe the time series and the recovery, not only the final average.
The player may also retain stale decoded frames after the transport has recovered. Measure network arrival time and actual display time independently where possible.

title: 10  Debugging
section: Turn a symptom into a test
text:
Turn a symptom into a test
Suppose the picture freezes while audio continues. Start by writing two facts: audio is still being presented; video is not. That narrows the investigation, but it does not prove the network is healthy. Audio may need less bandwidth, and the two media paths may have different queues.








Question
If yes
If no




Are new video objects arriving?
Inspect parsing and decoding
Inspect the video subscription and publisher


Are decoded video frames being produced?
Inspect presentation timing and rendering
Check configuration and missing reference pictures


Does the displayed frame age keep increasing?
Inspect queued work and adaptation
Check whether the player is skipping or pausing instead



Take these observations over the same interval. A decoder counter from a minute ago cannot explain whether new objects are usable now. If your library exposes no counter for a stage, add a small log at that boundary rather than treating the missing measurement as zero.

title: 10  Debugging
section: Collect evidence that connects the layers
text:
Collect evidence that connects the layers
For a useful bug report, record the client and relay versions, actual transport, publication and track identifiers, codec, error code, and the time of the failure. Include the smallest repeatable sequence that triggers it.
QUIC packet captures do not normally expose encrypted application payloads. Structured application logs and transport telemetry such as qlog can provide information that packet timing alone cannot. If your implementation exports a supported qlog trace, qvis provides QUIC visualizations for inspecting transport behavior. A transport trace still does not show whether the player presented a frame. Redact credentials and private publication names before sharing evidence.
One final habit helps: change one thing at a time. If you replace the codec, relay, browser, and network together, a successful run will leave you with four possible explanations.

title: 11  Frequently Asked Questions
text:
Is MoQ a finished standard?
These questions connect ideas from several chapters: which applications MoQ suits, how it relates to other protocols, and what its reliability and compatibility claims mean. Each answer gives the main point first and links to a fuller explanation where useful.
You can read this chapter in any order. For a term rather than a design question, use the glossary.
The baseline for this edition is draft-ietf-moq-transport-21, dated September 8, 2026. At the research date, it is an active Internet-Draft rather than a published RFC. Treat wire details as versioned and check the current IETF document status before implementing them.
This book is a dated explanation, not an automatically synchronized mirror of the specification. Links to the pinned draft preserve what the edition describes. Links to project documentation can change after publication.

title: 11  Frequently Asked Questions
text:
Does MoQ replace WebRTC?
MoQ is an alternative for some applications, rather than a universal replacement for WebRTC. For a side-by-side introduction, see How does MoQ compare with WebRTC?.
The two can serve some of the same applications. Consider our lecture: a conversation between the lecturer and a student, and delivery to a large listening audience, are different parts of the same experience. Either technology may be used in a larger system that supports both.
In a browser, WebRTC provides much of the encoding, transmission, and receiving machinery together. A MoQ implementation supplies named-content delivery; its media library supplies the capture, codec, and playback pieces above it. Compare complete systems on the devices and network paths your audience uses. The protocol name alone does not tell you the delay or operating cost.

title: 11  Frequently Asked Questions
section: Does it replace HLS or DASH?
text:
Does it replace HLS or DASH?
HLS (HTTP Live Streaming) and DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) describe ways for players to obtain media in pieces over HTTP, the protocol used for web requests. A description of the available media tells the player which pieces to request. This fits established web servers and caching infrastructure. The DASH Industry Forum’s architecture overview describes DASH’s presentation description and segment model.
MoQ instead lets a receiver subscribe to a named track and receive objects as they become available. Both approaches need media formats, players, and a policy for adapting to the network. Neither the use of HTTP nor subscription by itself fixes the final playback delay. HLS’s playlist-and-segment model is described in RFC 8216, section 2; MoQ subscriptions are described in draft-21, section 3.1.
A service can use more than one delivery path. The moq.dev project includes gateways for established formats and protocols. A gateway is a concrete integration to test, not evidence that every arbitrary MoQ publication is playable by an HLS player.

title: 11  Frequently Asked Questions
section: Why would I cancel a reliable stream?
text:
Why would I cancel a reliable stream?
Reliability repairs missing bytes; it does not decide whether you still want them. Suppose the viewer has fallen behind and the player can restart from a newer, independently decodable group. Spending more time repairing an older group may prolong the delay. The delivery policy can stop that old work while retaining reliable delivery for work that is still useful.
The receiver also needs to discard its stale playback queue and resume at a valid point. Cancellation alone cannot make a player catch up. Latency and Congestion follows those decisions.
This also answers a common question: is all MoQ traffic unreliable? No. An active QUIC stream provides reliable, ordered bytes. Datagrams are a separate option: QUIC does not retransmit them when they are lost. QUIC and WebTransport explains the distinction.

title: 11  Frequently Asked Questions
section: Can I send chat or game state?
text:
Can I send chat or game state?
The payload model is not limited to media. But your data still needs a design that matches loss, ordering, and late joining. A fresh state snapshot can replace an old one. An isolated “increment score” event often cannot.
For an illustrative game, put a full state snapshot at a restart boundary and define how later updates relate to it. If you need an authoritative event history, provide persistence and recovery deliberately rather than assuming a live track is a database.

title: 11  Frequently Asked Questions
text:
Is MoQ peer-to-peer?
MOQT can operate between endpoints or through relays. It does not by itself supply every rendezvous and NAT traversal mechanism needed for arbitrary browser-to-browser connectivity. The common browser deployment connects outward to a server through WebTransport.
Some native stacks add their own peer connectivity. Those are implementation capabilities to investigate separately from the core object and subscription model.

title: 11  Frequently Asked Questions
section: Is moq-lite the same as MOQT?
text:
Is moq-lite the same as MOQT?
No. moq-lite uses a simpler model, and the moq.dev stack documents compatibility paths for specified MOQT versions. Compatibility depends on the negotiated revision, supported features, and media format. Two products carrying “MoQ” in their name are not an interoperability test.

title: 11  Frequently Asked Questions
section: Can I use this book as a specification?
text:
Can I use this book as a specification?
Use it to understand the problems and vocabulary. Use the exact applicable protocol draft for normative behavior, and the documentation for the library version you ship. The walkthrough commands are sourced examples, not a claim that every supported platform was tested.

title: 12  Glossary
text:
Authentication and authorization
Use this chapter to look up a term while reading. Related terms are grouped together, and the groups are ordered alphabetically by their headings. Each group links to the chapter that explains how the ideas work together.
These definitions describe this book’s usage. The same word can mean different things at different layers; the linked specification supplies the exact protocol definition.
Authentication: establishing which identity an endpoint or user has.
Authorization: deciding what that identity may do, such as publishing a lecture or subscribing to it.
End-to-end encryption: content protection whose keys are held by the intended content endpoints, so an intermediate relay cannot read the protected payload. Routing metadata can remain visible.
Read more in Security and Access.

title: 12  Glossary
text:
Broadcast and catalog
Broadcast: in moq.dev terminology, a named collection of tracks belonging to a publication. Do not assume the word refers to network broadcast packets.
Catalog: media metadata describing the available tracks or renditions and how to decode them. The format and schema depend on the media layer in use.
Read more in Media and the Browser.

title: 12  Glossary
text:
Codec, container, and timestamp
Codec: a method for encoding and decoding media. The codec compresses pictures or sound; the transport delivers the resulting bytes.
Container: a framing format that packages encoded media with information needed to interpret it, such as timestamps. It is distinct from the codec.
Timestamp: a position on a media timeline. It is not automatically a wall-clock time or a measurement of network delay.
Read more in Media and the Browser.

title: 12  Glossary
text:
Connection and session
Connection: the underlying transport relationship between endpoints. With relays, a publisher and viewer generally do not share a single end-to-end QUIC connection.
Session: the MoQ protocol relationship operating over a transport. Successful transport setup does not imply successful protocol initialization or authorization.
Read more in QUIC and WebTransport.

title: 12  Glossary
text:
IP, TCP, UDP, and QUIC
IP: the Internet Protocol, which addresses packets and supports forwarding between networks.
TCP: a transport providing a reliable, ordered byte stream in each direction of a connection.
UDP: a transport carrying separate datagrams without built-in retransmission or ordering.
QUIC: a secure transport over UDP with multiple ordered byte streams and connection-level congestion control.
Packet: a network transmission unit. Packet boundaries do not define MoQ object boundaries.
ACK: an acknowledgment of transport reception, not proof of decoding or playback.
RTT: round-trip time, a measure of network delay to a peer and back.
Read the networking introduction and comparison tables.

title: 12  Glossary
text:
Keyframe and rendition
Keyframe: in this guide’s simplified video examples, a picture providing a fresh decoding starting point. Exact random-access behavior depends on the codec and packaging.
Rendition: an alternative encoding of content, such as a lower-resolution video. Receiving two renditions does not mean their decoder state is interchangeable.
Read more in Media and the Browser.

title: 12  Glossary
text:
Latency, jitter, and congestion
Latency: delay between specified events. Always ask which events: packet send and receipt, capture and display, or another pair.
Jitter: variation in delay. A playback buffer can absorb some variation at the cost of additional latency.
Congestion: a condition where demand exceeds available network capacity, causing queues or loss. Application queues can also grow when production outpaces delivery.
Read more in Latency and Congestion.

title: 12  Glossary
text:
MOQT, moq-lite, and hang
MOQT: Media over QUIC Transport, the IETF publish/subscribe protocol described by a versioned draft in this edition.
moq-lite: the smaller protocol model used by the moq.dev project, with implementation-specific compatibility support.
hang: the moq.dev media layer providing catalog and container conventions above its generic transport model.
Read more in What, Why, and How.

title: 12  Glossary
text:
Object, group, and subgroup
Object: an addressable payload in MOQT. Its identity includes its track, group ID, and object ID. An object is not necessarily a video frame.
Group: a collection of objects within a track. A media format can arrange groups as independent join points; the group boundary alone does not guarantee that the contained media can be decoded.
Subgroup: a delivery grouping of objects within one group, sent in ascending object-ID order on its subgroup stream. Stream-based subscription delivery carries a subgroup on a subgroup stream; FETCH uses its own stream representation. This is part of MOQT’s model and is omitted from moq-lite’s simpler model.
Read more in Tracks, Groups, and Objects.

title: 12  Glossary
text:
Publisher, subscriber, and relay
Publisher: an endpoint that supplies requested objects. An original publisher first introduces the content.
Subscriber: an endpoint requesting and receiving a track.
Relay: an intermediary acting as subscriber upstream and publisher downstream. It forwards content and may cache objects.
Read more in Relays and Distribution.

title: 12  Glossary
text:
Stream and datagram
Stream: here, usually a reliable ordered QUIC or WebTransport byte stream. A “live stream” in everyday speech is a different concept.
Datagram: an independently delivered message without QUIC retransmission on loss. It does not promise arrival or order and has a size limit.
Read more in QUIC and WebTransport.

title: 12  Glossary
text:
Track and namespace
Track: the named sequence of groups a subscriber can request. Audio and each video rendition can use separate tracks.
Namespace: the structured naming context for tracks. In MOQT, fields are byte sequences, not necessarily human-readable path components.
Read more in Publishing and Subscribing.

Read the object model before the wire-message tables. Once tracks and groups make sense, the fields become answers to recognizable problems rather than an arbitrary list of integers.

title: 13  References and Reading
section: A route through the MOQT specification
text:
A route through the MOQT specification
Start with the question you are trying to answer. These links all refer to draft-21, so their terminology and section numbers belong to the same edition.



Question
Where to read




What identifies a piece of content?
Objects (§2.1) and track naming (§2.4.1)


How do groups and subgroups organize it?
Subgroups (§2.2) and groups (§2.3)


How do I follow new content or request older objects?
Subscriptions (§3.1), fetch (§3.2), and joining an ongoing track (§3.5)


How are publications discovered?
Namespace discovery (§4)


Which work gets sent first, and when does it stop?
Priorities (§5.1) and delivery timeouts (§5.2)


What happens when peers connect?
Session establishment (§6.2), initialization (§6.3), and stream usage (§6.4)


What can a relay retain and forward?
Caching relays (§7.1) and relay object handling (§7.7)



Read the explanatory sections first, then use control messages (§9) when you need field layouts. The words MUST, SHOULD, and MAY express requirement levels when a specification adopts BCP 14, which comprises RFC 2119 and RFC 8174. In particular, a recommendation is not a guarantee that every implementation will behave identically.

title: 13  References and Reading
text:
The transport underneath
RFC 9000 defines QUIC’s transport, including streams, flow control, and cancellation. RFC 9001 describes its use of TLS. RFC 9002 covers loss detection and congestion control.
RFC 9221 defines the QUIC DATAGRAM extension. Read it when deciding whether a small payload should be retried or replaced, and when checking message-size constraints.

title: 13  References and Reading
text:
Browser interfaces
The W3C WebTransport specification describes the browser API for streams and datagrams. Its presence does not remove the need for a protocol library above it.
The W3C WebCodecs specification describes low-level codec interfaces. It is useful for understanding decoder configuration and frame ownership. It does not define a full media player.

title: 13  References and Reading
text:
The WebRTC comparison
The early comparison uses the W3C WebRTC specification for the browser interface. The network behavior comes from IETF documents: RFC 8835, section 3.4 covers connection establishment with ICE and relay support, while section 3.5 identifies the media and data transports.
For media, WebRTC uses SRTP, the secure form of the Real-time Transport Protocol. Data channels use SCTP, the Stream Control Transmission Protocol, carried inside DTLS, Datagram Transport Layer Security. You do not need to learn these packet formats to understand the comparison; the distinction is that WebRTC specifies how these pieces fit together for real-time communication.
RFC 7667, section 3.7 explains selective-forwarding media servers. It supports the important point that a WebRTC conference can distribute media through a server; it need not connect every participant directly to every other participant.

title: 13  References and Reading
text:
The moq.dev implementation
Start with moq.dev and the concepts guide. Then read the separate explanations of moq-lite, hang, and transport choices.
For experiments, use the setup and development documentation. For a reachable relay, read the production guide. These pages describe a particular project and can evolve independently of this book’s IETF baseline.

title: 13  References and Reading
text:
Editorial approach and limitations
The protocol baseline was reviewed on September 16, 2026; the technical explanations and linked setup resources were checked on September 22, 2026. The guide emphasizes stable ideas and avoids presenting a moving wire format as permanent. Draft-sensitive explanations refer to draft-21; implementation-specific examples are labeled with the project name.
This guide does not claim measured performance results, exhaustive browser compatibility, or successful execution of the upstream walkthrough. The latency values are invented examples. Validate a chosen stack and revision in your own deployment before relying on particular behavior.

title: 13  References and Reading
text:
Keeping an edition accurate
When updating the book, record the new research date and protocol revision together. Review terminology, setup, subscription behavior, timeout semantics, and the media-format boundary before changing the edition badge.
Keep examples identified as examples. If you add benchmarks, publish the workload, hardware, network conditions, implementation versions, and measurement points. If you add runnable SDK code, pin dependencies and verify it against the corresponding relay. An explanation is most useful when readers can tell exactly what it establishes.
